Egypt reaffirms its rejection to all Israeli practices seeking to displace Palestinian people from their land, to deny their right to return, and to deny their right to reparations. We also reaffirm that the only means of ensuring peace and stability in our region will begin by implementing the two-state solution. the creation of a Palestinian state in 1967 borders with East Jerusalem as its capital. In this regard, we wish to thank and congratulate all States who recently recognized the State of Palestine, which is an important step for peace and justice. We urge other States to follow suit and to recognize the State of Palestine and to express their solidarity with the Palestinian people in its legitimate quest for peace. We support the President Trump plan for peace and security in the Middle East. In the same vein, Egypt will continue its intensive work regionally and internationally to stop the war in Gaza and to ensure urgent humanitarian access that is untrammeled for our Palestinian brothers in accordance with our unflagging commitment to national and humanitarian law to help the Palestinian people. Mr. Chairman, hate speech and incitation to hatred is one of the biggest threats internationally today. This hate speech transcends national boundaries, and its spread on digital and media platforms. This poses a threat to peace, to societies, and it undermines peaceful coexistence among religions and cultures. Certain groups are targeted increasingly, including Muslims. This exacerbates the crisis, and fighting effectively all forms of discrimination, intolerance, and Islamophobia, and hatred and intolerance needs to be a priority for the international community. We have agreed on actions in accordance with the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights. Article 20 of this international pact seeks to combat this violence, although the phenomenon continues to gain ground, which is disturbing. We welcome the nomination of the Special Representative of the Secretary-General against Islamophobia. This is an important stage which shows that the United Nations is cognizant of the extent of this threat to international peace and security. We wish him every success, and we're hoping to work closely together with him in order to strengthen the peaceful coexistence among peoples and religions. Mr. Chair, in closing, Egypt will continue to strengthen and promote human rights in all areas through the special mechanisms of the United Nations, above all through the UPR. That is a platform for international negotiation. platform that is centered on the protection of human rights. And in this world, we are encountering major challenges to international peace and security, these challenges also against development and prosperity for everyone, and challenges to the promotion of human rights. I thank you, Chairman.
I thank the distinguished representative of Egypt. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Cyprus.

Thank you, Chair. At the outset, allow me to extend my best wishes to you, the Bureau and the Secretariat of the Third Committee for a fruitful and constructive term. And Cyprus fully aligns itself with the statement delivered by the European Union, but allow me to add a few remarks in my national capacity. Mr. Chair, Cyprus considers human rights as the cornerstone for the multilateral system has made human rights top priority in its foreign policy. Thus, Cyprus' election for the very first time as a member of the Human Rights Council for the period 2025-2027 has been a distinct honor. We are firmly committed to promoting, protecting, and implementing human rights at national and international level, as well as advancing and strengthening human rights within the United Nations system. Regrettably, the The people of Cyprus have experienced for the last 51 years gross violation of their human rights and fundamental freedoms as a result of the illegal Turkish military invasion and continued military occupation of 37% of the territory of the Republic of Cyprus. More than one third of the population is still internally displaced, being denied the right to return and peacefully enjoy their properties. Instead, their land is subjugated and subjected to unlawful exploitation by the occupation regime. Equally alarming is the occupying power's systematic policy of demographic engineering through the mass transfer of settlers, which constitutes a war crime under international humanitarian law. Cyprus's cultural and religious heritage has also suffered irreparable loss, with over 500 churches looted, desecrated, or destroyed. The intentional destruction of cultural heritage is recognized as a violation of international law and under the Rome Statute as a war crime. The few hundred enclaved Greek Cypriots and Maronites who remain in the occupied areas continue to face oppression and discrimination, including restrictions on education, religion and access to their communities. At the same time, the fate of nearly half of the missing persons in Cyprus remains unresolved due to the refusal of Turkiye to provide to the Committee on Missing Persons all relevant information from its military archives and grant unhindered access to what it classifies as military areas. And in recounting the violations committed, it is equally important to acknowledge the restrictions suffered by the Turkish Cypriots living under occupation. Their freedom of expression, thought, religion and association are curtailed. Their daily lives are subjected to surveillance, interference, and their culture and identity are suppressed. Mr. Chair, recent developments further underscore the severity of the situation. On July 19, five elderly Greek Cypriots were unlawfully detained and illegally charged by the occupying regime for visiting their properties in the occupied areas of Cyprus. They were subjected to inhumane treatment, leading to severe health deterioration, and, while released under conditions, remain barred from returning to their homes. We strongly condemn this politically motivated detention, which amounts to kidnapping and hostage taking. Human rights violations cannot be normalised because of the passage of time, and Cyprus will continue to raise these issues until the rights and freedoms of all Cypriots are fully restored. Mr Chair, around the world, women and girls continue to face discrimination, violence and economic marginalisation, while systemic barriers and global crises risk eroding hard-won progress. As we mark the 30th anniversary since the landmark adoption of the Beijing Declaration and Platform of Action, this is not just a moment for reflection. It's an opportunity to accelerate action and reaffirm our joint commitment towards gender equality and the empowerment of all women and girls. Cyprus is fully committed in intensifying all efforts towards achieving gender equality, eliminating all forms of discrimination against women and girls, promoting, protecting and fulfilling their rights, as well as providing equal opportunities for their full, equal and meaningful participation in all spheres of life. Cyprus has taken concrete steps and measures in this regard by strengthening legislative frameworks and implementing gender-responsive budgeting, as well as public campaigns to combat stereotypes. Chair, trafficking in persons is a heinous crime and a serious global issue affecting millions of people worldwide. Human dignity is non-negotiable, trafficking in persons can no longer be tolerated. Combating trafficking in persons, protecting victims, prosecuting perpetrators, and strengthening partnerships to enhance coordination and cooperation is amongst the top priorities of the Cyprus government. And as such, it has been a great honor for Cyprus to be appointed by the President of the 79th session of the GA as co-facilitator. together with Tajikistan to produce a political declaration on the implementation of the United Nations Global Plan of Action to combat trafficking in persons. And we look forward to the relevant high-level meeting of the General Assembly to be held this coming November. Mr. Chairman, Cyprus reaffirmed its strong commitment to the rights of the child as enshrined in the Convention of the Rights of the Child and its optional protocols. Relevant national initiatives, strategies and policies have been adopted. while the Independent Commissioner for the Protection of the Rights of the Child plays a central role in monitoring legislation and amplifying children's voices. Cyprus is a strong supporter of the full, effective and meaningful participation of young persons in decision-making processes at all levels, local, national, regional and international, including here at the UN. The Government is implementing programmes and actions with a special focus on giving young persons the opportunity to shape our national policies and has institutionalised youth voices in national decision-making structures. We remain committed in ensuring that the voices of the young persons are not only asked for and heard, but are mainstreamed both nationally as well as across the UN system. Older persons are equally vital to society, contributing knowledge and experience. yet often face marginalisation and discrimination. Cyprus is committed to building an inclusive, age-friendly society that promotes independence, support and care. In this regard, Cyprus has adopted the first ever national strategy and action plan for active ageing. The protection of cultural diversity is intrinsically linked to the protection of human rights and fundamental freedoms. Culture in all its dimensions is deeply rooted in the very existence of all Cypriots and is one of Cyprus' top priorities. Moreover, during Cyprus' chairmanship of the Committee of Ministers of the Council of Europe, the Convention on Offences Relating to Cultural Property, also known as the Nicosia Convention, was adopted. This convention constitutes the first ever international legal text incorporating a criminal code for perpetrators who destroy, steal, or trade cultural heritage treasures. In keeping with this focus, Cyprus is one of the initiators and co-chairs of the UN Group of Friends of Culture, together with Egypt, Italy, Mexico and the United Arab Emirates. Mr. Chair, in conclusion, Cyprus reaffirms its unwavering commitment to the promotion and protection of human rights and fundamental freedoms for all. As a divided country under occupation, we will persist in raising the plight of Cypriots whose rights are violated. while remaining steadfast in advancing the rights of women, children and young persons. And we stand ready to work constructively with all Member States and the Organization to strengthen multilateralism and ensure a just, peaceful and prosperous world for the current and future generations. I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Cyprus. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Rwanda.

Thank you, Mr. Chair. Mr. Chair, on behalf of Rwanda, allow me to congratulate you and the Bureau on your election, and you can count on Rwanda's constructive engagement throughout this session. My delegation aligns itself with the statements delivered on behalf of the African Group, as well as G77 and China. In my national capacity, I wish to highlight Rwanda's perspectives on social development, the advancement of women, and the promotion and protection of human rights. Mr. Chair. Rwanda's national transformation has always placed human development at the core of our journey. In just two decades, Rwanda has cut poverty by more than half, from 58.9% in 2001 to 27.4% in 2024, and we reduced extreme poverty in one of the fastest poverty declines recorded in Africa within a single generation. Strategic investments in health, education, and social protection, notably Rwanda's community-based health insurance, now covering over 90% of the population, have propelled life expectancy upward from 49 to nearly 70 years since 2000. Additionally, education has remained a cornerstone of opportunity with universal primary enrollment above 98% and sustained gender parity in both primary and secondary schools. Initiatives such as nine-year and 12-year basic education continue to equip children with a foundation for a better future, while technical and vocational training has expanded to prepare young people for a rapidly modernizing labor market. With over 60% of our population under 25, Rwanda sees youth as a defining strength. The National Youth Council, enshrined in our constitution, ensures young people have a direct voice in governance, budgeting, and decision-making, ensuring that our transformation is not only for youth, but driven by youth too. Mr. Chair, the 30th anniversary of the Beijing Declaration and Platform for Action holds special meaning for Rwanda. Adopted just one year after the genocide against the Tutsi, it provides a blueprint for rebuilding our society. Today, gender equality is firmly embedded in our governance. And beyond world-leading parliamentary representation, the Rwandan woman's leadership extends now to major financial and public sector institutions, as exemplified by our Speaker of Parliament, Chief Justice, Prosecutor General, and the governor of the central bank. As such, the economic empowerment of women has also advanced. 96% of women are financially included through cooperatives and mobile banking. Women represent 46.2% of STEM students and 43.2% in technical and vocational training, supported by deliberate policies to close gender gaps. Land ownership by women has increased to 26% of registered land solely by women, unlocking access to credit and investments. Health gains have also followed. Between 2015 and 2020, maternal mortality fell from 210 to 203 per 100,000 live births. Skilled birth attendants rose from 91% to 94%, with 93% of births now taking place in health facilities underpinned by universal health coverage. Rwanda's solidarity extends beyond our borders. When conflict erupted in Kabul, Rwanda welcomed the All-Girls School of Leadership Afghanistan, enabling Afghan girls to continue their education in safety. This reflects our conviction that empowering women and girls is a global responsibility. Mr. Chair, human rights are the foundation of Rwanda's national rebirth. After the 1994 genocide against the Tutsi, Rwanda abolished the death penalty. We established the National Commission for Human Rights, and we strengthened independent accountability institutions. We also continue to welcome and host UN special rapporteurs to observe progress on the ground, demonstrating our transparency and steadfast commitment to the protection of rights. Equally, Rwanda believes the Human Rights Council must remain above politicization to preserve its credibility and the very purpose for which Member States established it. The Universal Periodic Review remains the most credible and universally accepted mechanism to assess human rights, ensuring objectivity and fairness. The Universal Periodic Review exemplifies transparency, accountability, and constructive dialogue, offering all member states equal treatment. This impartial process builds trust, strengthens credibility, and fosters collective responsibility for advancing human rights globally. Rwanda remains committed to working through these mechanisms to promote rights without bias, without politicization, and with integrity. Mr. Chair, Rwanda is deeply concerned when some states position themselves as arbiters of human rights while disproportionately scrutinizing African nations through selective or politicized reporting. Rwanda firmly rejects such approaches. Human rights must never be weaponized for political leverage or narrow interests. As we celebrate eight years of our organization, it is high time that states who politicize human rights end such practices and instead embrace the spirit of mutual cooperation necessary to advance shared values and prosperity. As I conclude, Mr. Chair, allow me to reaffirm Rwanda's steadfast commitment to social development, gender equality, and the promotion and protection of human rights. We believe progress is best achieved through cooperation, dialogue, and shared responsibility, guided by impartial and transparent multilateral processes. As we continue building a society rooted in unity and inclusivity, Rwanda stands ready to share its experiences, to learn from others, and contribute constructively to global efforts. I thank you, Mr. Chair.
I thank the distinguished representative of Rwanda. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Liechtenstein.

Mr. Chair, let me start by underlining that human rights are one of the three central pillars of the United Nations, alongside peace and security and sustainable development. As we look ahead to the UN80 process and beyond, we must ensure that all of our actions are firmly grounded in this understanding. Upholding and advancing human rights is not an optional component, but an essential foundation for everything we do to strengthen the organization's relevance and effectiveness in the years to come. Mr. Chair, human rights are among the earliest and most serious casualties of conflict. When peace and security is eroded, entire populations are deprived of their most basic rights, including, most notably, the right to life. While the illegal use of force is a clear human rights violation and needs to be recognized as such, all armed conflict magnify patterns of abuse that strike at the core of human dignity. Enforced disappearance, torture, unlawful detention, and sexual and gender-based violence are among the most frequent violations documented in armed conflict in recent years. The aggression against Ukraine, the devastation in Gaza, and the ongoing war in Sudan are indeed reminders of how conflict not only claims lives but enables systematic and widespread human rights violations. The impact of such violations falls overwhelmingly on civilians. Schools, hospitals, and places of worship, protected under international law, are destroyed, cutting off communities from essential services and leaving long-term scars on generations. For certain sectors of society, women, children, older persons, and persons with disabilities, the consequences are often more severe and enduring. These realities show clearly that protecting civilians is not only a humanitarian necessity, but also a human rights imperative. To ensure accountability for war crimes, along with the other core crimes, and put an end to cycle of violence fueled by impunity, we continue to support the International Criminal Court in carrying out its mandate independently and with impartiality. Mr. Chair, too many children across the world are still deprived of their rights to grow up in safety, to learn, and to play. Nowhere is this more apparent than in situations of armed conflict. The Secretary-General's most recent annual report documented a further rise in grave violations, with 2024 marking yet another year of an alarming trend. Children continue to be killed and maimed at unprecedented levels, schools and hospitals are repeatedly attacked, and the denial of humanitarian access leaves countless children without essential protection and care. Liechtenstein reiterates its strong support for ensuring the independence and integrity of the mandate of the Special Representative for Children in Armed Conflict, as well as its monitoring and reporting mechanism on violations against children. As the Secretary-General and his Special Representative have repeatedly underlined, these instruments have proven effective in changing the behavior of conflict parties and strengthening the protection of children. In the spirit of the Prove It Matters initiative, we wish to recall our global commitment to protect children's rights in conflict. Only by upholding the Convention on the Rights of the Child and its Optional Protocols and ensuring accountability for grave violations committed against children can we protect them from the horrors of war and make their rights a reality and not an aspiration. Mr. Chair, this year marks two landmark anniversaries for gender equality and women's rights, the 30th anniversary of the Beijing Declaration and Platform for Action, and the 25th anniversary of the Women, Peace, and Security Agenda. Both frameworks remain transformative blueprints, Beijing +30 for advancing the full participation and empowerment of women and girls in all spheres of life, and WPS for recognizing women's indispensable role in conflict prevention, peacebuilding, and recovery. Yet despite progress, implementation gaps persist with women still underrepresented in decision making and disproportionately affected by conflict and crises. Women's inclusion and leadership are not only critical objectives for gender equality, but also vital for ensuring more just and equitable governance. For the first time in the history of Liechtenstein, both the Prime Minister and the Deputy Prime Minister are women, a milestone in our political landscape. We strongly believe that greater representation of women in senior positions benefits everyone, including in this very institution. Mr. Chair, the UN system can only fully and effectively deliver on its human rights mandate with the necessary financial means. As the donor with the highest per capita contributions, Liechtenstein remains committed to supporting the important work of the Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights, which already relies heavily on voluntary funding. The human rights pillar has historically received less than 7% of the UN's regular budget and less than 1% of overall UN expenditure. While we strongly support the efforts by the Secretary General to strengthen the efficiency and effectiveness of this organization through the UN80 initiative, We are concerned about the proposed disproportionate cuts to the already underfunded human rights pillar and the revised 2026 budget. These cuts will result in financial savings, but also risk having significant consequences for those relying on the work of the UN, including the Independent Investigative Mechanism for Myanmar and the International Impartial and Independent Mechanism for Syria. Adequate funding for the Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights and for UN human rights mechanisms is essential not only for justice and accountability, but also for the UN's credibility and for the effectiveness of its work in peace, security, and development. Mr. Chair, human trafficking and modern slavery remain among the gravest human rights violations of our time, affecting an estimated 50 million people worldwide. The latest report by the Special Rapporteur on Contemporary Forms of Slavery underscores that financial sector actors can either enable or prevent these crimes through their operations, investments, and business relationships. Liechtenstein welcomes this timely focus, which directly complements our longstanding commitment to mobilizing finance as a force for accountability and change through the Finance Against Slavery and Trafficking Initiative. It has been instrumental in providing the financial sector with the tools, standards, and collaborative platforms necessary to detect and disrupt illicit financial flows derived from modern slavery and human trafficking, to integrate anti-slavery measures into investment and lending practices, and to promote survivor-centered approaches to financial inclusion. As highlighted in the report, multi-stakeholder cooperation, robust disclosure, and due diligence frameworks, as well as survivor protection, must go hand in hand if financial markets are to become drivers of prevention and remedy. Liechtenstein remains convinced that by aligning global finance with the fight against slavery, we can address not only symptoms but root causes, reducing vulnerabilities, closing off avenues for illicit profit, and ensuring that survivors are reintegrated with dignity. Mr. Chair, self-determination is both a prerequisite for the full enjoyment of human rights and a complex but fundamental aspect of state sovereignty, often involving a tension between the rights of people and the stability of existing states. Liechtenstein is a firm supporter of the right to self-determination, a cornerstone of the UN Charter. Self-determination must also be understood in context where communities seek to freely determine their political status within a nation state. Too often, conflicts arise from inadequate or repressive state responses to communities, including minority groups, calling for greater internal self-determination, whether through autonomy, self-governance, or self-administration. A more nuanced understanding of these dynamics is essential to prevent political tensions from escalating into armed conflict or secession. Mr. Chair, international human rights law obliges states to protect and promote the rights of all people without discrimination. Yet around the world, individuals continue to face criminalization, stigma, and violence based on their sexual orientation, gender identity, or sex characteristics. In Liechtenstein, we took an important step forward this year when marriage equality entered into force, following last year's near anonymous vote in parliament on that subject. We are committed to strengthen the rights and the protection of LGBTIQ+ persons. To this end, Liechtenstein has recently joined the UN LGBTI Core Group as an observer. We very much look forward to working with other delegations towards the promotion of equality within the UN system. Our societies can only reach their full potential when we recognize diversity as a source of strength in our daily interactions and the way our political and legal institutions uphold the dignity of every individual. I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Liechtenstein. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Singapore.

Thank you very much, Mr. Chair. Let me begin by congratulating you on your election as Chair to this very important Committee, and we are especially pleased and proud to see a fellow ASEAN country chairing this very important Committee. I would also like to commend you and your Bureau members for your very transparent and inclusive consultations on the programme of work for the Committee this year. We very much support your approach. My thanks also to our long-serving secretariat and Secretary of the Committee for their hard work for this year. Mr. Chair, human rights have always been a fundamental pillar of the UN's work, and we have always in Singapore realised the inextricable link between human rights and sustainable development, as well as the link between human rights and the dignity of all people. The principles enshrined in the UN Charter and the Universal Declaration of Human Rights are foundational to every society, government, and of course, to the United Nations and to the work in this Committee. As a country, Singapore has always been committed to building a just and inclusive society for our people, one that is tailored to our historical, social, and cultural context. We are committed to protecting the rights, dignity, safety and welfare of all Singaporeans. Our approach is based on a pragmatic ethos that aims to improve the lives and livelihoods of all our people in meaningful and tangible ways. Mr. Chair, the 30th anniversary of the Beijing Declaration and Platform for Action this year is a timely reminder of the urgent need to redress gender inequality. In this context, Singapore reaffirms its unwavering commitment to the Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination Against Women and our support for Sustainable Development Goal 5 on gender equality. Singapore has always placed gender equality and the empowerment of women and girls at the centre of our policies. There can only be meaningful development when women fully participate in society and the economy. We are pleased that today, we are ranked number 8 in the UN Human Development Report's Gender Inequality Index. Since the launch of our White Paper on Women's Development in 2022, Singapore has strengthened our legislation to protect the rights of women at home and in workplaces. In 2023, we amended the Women's Charter to empower victim-survivors of family violence to better protect themselves through restraining orders. This year, we passed the Workplace Fairness Legislation, which prohibits unfair employment decisions based on protected characteristics such as sex, marital status, pregnancy, and caregiving responsibilities. But our efforts extend beyond legislation. At a societal level, we are also inculcating new norms rooted in respect and partnership. This includes encouraging greater shared parental responsibility in caregiving by doubling government-paid paternity leave and strengthening public education to break gender stereotypes. Singapore is also working towards enabling persons with disabilities to fully contribute to society, in line with our commitments under the Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities. We have strengthened social protection services for persons with disabilities to enable them to live more independently. We have also introduced enhanced financial subsidies for long-term disability care services, and schemes for persons with disabilities to build up their retirement savings earlier to safeguard their long-term financial security. These efforts reflect Singapore's conviction that every individual deserves to live with dignity, security and equal opportunity. Mr. Chair, this principle of inclusion underpins our journey as a country. Our Constitution mandates the principle of non-discrimination that all persons are equal before the law. The Presidential Council for Minority Rights ensures that our laws do not contain any discriminatory provisions against racial or religious minorities. Today, Singapore is one of the most diverse and harmonious societies in the world. A 2014 Pew Research Center report ranked Singapore as the most religiously diverse country, while a recent A poll by Gallup World Poll found Singapore to be among the top of countries for tolerance and existence and peaceful coexistence between ethnic minorities. Mr. Chair, another issue that I would like to address is crime prevention, which is critical for the promotion and protection of human rights, as it ensures a safe environment where all individuals can enjoy their rights and freedoms. Singapore was named the world's safest country in Gallup's 2025 Global Safety Report. This is the result of considered policies to counter various transnational crimes, including cybercrime as well as drug trafficking. Given the increasingly cross-border nature of criminal activities, Singapore works closely with our international law enforcement counterparts to disrupt criminal networks and recover criminal proceeds. Another pervasive transnational threat is the scourge of drug abuse. As an international hub located near major drug production centres, Singapore is highly vulnerable to an inflow of illicit drugs. Nevertheless, we will not waver in our mission to achieve a society free of drug abuse to ensure health, safety and security of our people. We believe that harm prevention is crucial, and we have adopted an evidence-based approach to drug control, comprising preventive education, strict laws, rigorous enforcement, and effective rehabilitation. At the international level, Singapore will continue to support the impartial work of the UN Commission on Drugs and Crimes, and the International Narcotics Control Board and Commission on Narcotic Drugs. And as a member of the CND, Singapore will do its part through capacity building and the sharing of scientific expertise. Mr. Chair, to conclude, Singapore believes that it is incumbent on all governments to remain accountable, exercise good governance, and uphold the rule of law to advance the rights of its people. We are pleased that we rank well in various reports, including the World Justice Project's Rule of Law Index, as well as the World Bank's 2023 Worldwide Governance Indicators Index. That said, we recognise that what has worked for Singapore may not necessarily work for other countries. And in seeking to advance dialogue on human rights, it is therefore important to have a dialogue based on mutual respect and mutual understanding. Singapore is very much committed to having this dialogue based on mutual respect here at the United Nations, and in that spirit, we are ready to work with all our friends in this important committee. I thank you very much for your attention.

I thank the distinguished representative of Singapore. We have heard the last speaker on my list for this morning meeting. The committee will continue its general debate in the afternoon promptly at 3:00 p.m. The first three speakers are reflected in the live list, which has been circulated on the e-delegate portal. The meeting is adjourned.
